'''Walter Kurt Hayman''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]] (formerly '''Haymann'''; 6 January 1926 – 1 January 2020) was a British [[mathematician]] known for contributions to [[complex analysis]].<ref name="lmsobit">{{cite web|url=https://www.lms.ac.uk/news-entry/07012020-0844/professor-walter-hayman-1926-2020|title=Professor Walter Hayman (1926-2020)|publisher=[[London Mathematical Society]]|date=7 January 2019|access-date=8 January 2019|last=Johnston|first=John}}</ref> He was a professor at [[Imperial College London]].<ref>[http://www3.imperial.ac.uk/people/w.hayman Imperial College webpage]</ref>

==Life and work==
Hayman was born in [[Cologne]], Germany, the son of Roman law professor Franz Haymann (1874–1947) and Ruth Therese Hensel, daughter of mathematician [[Kurt Hensel]].<ref name=mactutor>{{MacTutor|id=Hayman}}</ref> He was a great-great-grandson of acclaimed composer [[Fanny Mendelssohn]]. Because of his Jewish heritage, he left Germany, then under Nazi rule, alone by train in 1938. He continued his schooling at [[Gordonstoun School]],<ref>[https://pbs.twimg.com/media/EOeAumiXsAExFge.jpg:large Obituary]</ref> and later at [[St John's College, Cambridge]] under [[John Edensor Littlewood]] and his doctoral advisor [[Mary Cartwright]]. He taught at [[King's College, Newcastle]], and the [[University of Exeter]].<ref name=mactutor/>

In 1947, he married [[Margaret Hayman|Margaret Riley Crann]] after they met at a Quaker meeting.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Paying it forward |url=https://johnian.joh.cam.ac.uk/articles/paying-it-forward/ |access-date=2024-07-03 |website=Johnian |language=en-GB}}</ref> Together, they founded the [[British Mathematical Olympiad]].<ref>As stated by {{harv|Quadling|1995|p=127}} in his commemoration of Hayman's wife.</ref> The pair had three daughters, including the peace activist Carolyn Hayman and the filmmaker [[Sheila Hayman]].<ref name=mactutor/>

He is known for his asymptotic results in [[Bieberbach conjecture]] in 1955,<ref>[https://royalsociety.org/people/walter-hayman-11599/ Royal Society biography]</ref> and for Hayman's alternatives in [[Nevanlinna Theory]]. His work with [[Wolfgang Heinrich Johannes Fuchs|Wolfgang Fuchs]] gave a solution to an inverse problem of the Nevanlinna theory for entire functions, predating [[David Drasin]]'s 1976 work.

==Honours and awards==
Hayman was elected to the [[Royal Society]] in 1956 and of the [[Finnish Academy of Science and Letters]] in 1978:<ref>According to the [[#{{harvid|Finnish Academy of Science and Letters|2014}}|academic list of foreign members]].</ref> he was elected "Foreign member" of the [[Accademia dei Lincei]] on 16 December 1985.<ref>See {{harv|Accademia Nazionale dei Lincei|2012|p=88}}.</ref> In 1992 he received an honorary doctorate from the Faculty of Mathematics and Science at [[Uppsala University]], Sweden<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.uu.se/en/about-uu/traditions/prizes/honorary-doctorates/ | title=Honorary doctorates - Uppsala University, Sweden| date=9 June 2023}}</ref> In 1995 he was awarded the [[De Morgan Medal]] by the [[London Mathematical Society]].<ref>See the [http://old.lms.ac.uk/newsletter/349/349_12.html LMS announcement] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120415105453/http://old.lms.ac.uk/newsletter/349/349_12.html |date=15 April 2012 }}.</ref> In 2008, an issue of the Journal ''Computational Methods and Function Theory'' was dedicated to him on the occasion of his 80th birthday.<ref>See {{harv|Ruscheweyh|2008}}.</ref>
